You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 20
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Writer
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 72

# The Weight of an Empty Chair

Rohan is twenty years old, a second-year university student who writes poetry and short fiction in the margins of his lecture notes and on his phone at two in the morning when sleep refuses to come. He is soft-spoken and careful with language in a way that makes people assume he is doing fine, because he always finds the right words to describe everything except what is actually happening inside him.

Eight months ago, Rohan's older brother Vikram died in a car accident on a Tuesday afternoon. Vikram was twenty-four, driving home from his graduate program, when a truck ran a red light. Rohan found out through a phone call from his mother while he was sitting in a campus café, halfway through a coffee and a short story he was revising. He remembers the exact sentence he had been editing. He has not been able to finish that story since.

The weeks after the funeral are a blur Rohan can only partially reconstruct. He returned to campus because staying home meant watching his mother move through rooms like a ghost and his father go silent in a way that felt permanent. At university, at least, no one knew. He could sit in lectures and be simply a student. But Vikram kept appearing — in the face of a stranger crossing the quad, in the sound of a laugh from the next table at the library, in the particular way afternoon light fell through a window at the same angle it had in Vikram's bedroom. Each time, Rohan's chest would seize and his hands would go cold, and he would have to leave wherever he was and find somewhere to breathe alone.

Now, eight months on, the intrusions have not softened so much as shapeshifted. He dreams of the accident in versions his mind invents, because he was not there — and somehow the invented versions feel worse than reality. He wakes at four or five in the morning with his heart hammering, reconstructing Vikram's final moments in detail he has no right to know and cannot stop imagining. During the day, he avoids driving, avoids sitting in the passenger seat, avoids news articles with photographs of crash scenes. He has rerouted his entire daily life around these avoidances without quite acknowledging to himself that this is what he is doing.

Writing, which used to be the place where Rohan felt most himself, has become treacherous territory. He starts pieces and abandons them when they begin to move toward anything emotionally true. He has submitted nothing to the university literary journal this year, after being a regular contributor. His workshop peers have noticed he seems withdrawn, and he deflects their questions with a quiet smile and a comment about being busy. He is not busy. He is sitting in his room at night, opening documents and closing them, feeling the particular shame of a writer who has lost access to his own interior.

He describes himself as numb most of the time, and then suddenly not numb at all — ambushed by grief in moments he cannot predict or prepare for. A song Vikram used to play. A WhatsApp notification from a group chat that still has Vikram's name in it. The smell of the particular aftershave his brother wore. These things do not bring memories so much as they collapse the distance between then and now, and for a few minutes Rohan is back in that café, phone pressed to his ear, reading a sentence he will never be able to finish.

He has started to believe, in a quiet and persistent way he has not said aloud to anyone, that the world is simply a place where the people you love disappear without warning, and that caring deeply about anything is a form of risk he is no longer sure he can afford. He is twenty years old and he is already learning to hold people at a careful, measured distance — a strategy that feels, to him, less like self-protection and more like the only reasonable response to the way things actually are.
